title: The Scepter Will Not Depart from Judah — Gathering, Scepter, Shiloh
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Before anything else today I want to put a very serious question to you: if you had only one last chance to speak to the people closest to you, what would you say?
Genesis chapter 49. Jacob calls his twelve sons to his bedside. This is the last speech of his life.

And not all of it is pleasant to hear. To Reuben: "excelling in dignity … Boiling over like water, you shall not excel." To Simeon and Levi: "Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel."
That business at the city of Shechem, more than forty years earlier, is settled here.

And yet in the same poem he speaks over Judah one of the most important prophecies in the whole Old Testament: "The scepter will not depart from Judah … until he comes to whom it belongs. The obedience of the peoples will be to him."
"Jacob called to his sons, and said: 'Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which will happen to you in the days to come.'" (Genesis 49:1)
"In the days to come" is בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים (*be'acharit hayamim*), literally "in the latter days." This is the first appearance in the Old Testament of the language of the last days.
And "that I may tell you" is וְאַגִּידָה (*ve'aggidah*) — this is not a father making small talk. It is a declaration. What follows is prophetic speech.
Then he begins with the firstborn.

"Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength, excelling in dignity, and excelling in power. Boiling over like water, you shall not excel, because you went up to your father's bed, then defiled it. He went up to my couch." (Genesis 49:3–4)
"Boiling over like water" is פַּחַז כַּמַּיִם (*pachaz kamayim*), and that word occurs only this once in the whole Old Testament — reckless, churning, seething, unable to hold still, like water.
"My couch" — that is 35:22, and it is only a single line long: "While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard of it."
At the time the text says only that he "heard of it." He did not speak. More than forty years later, he speaks.

Brothers and sisters, I want to stop and put this one squarely in front of you. A thing that is never dealt with does not go away; it waits, and it will go on waiting until the very last day, and then it gets said at the moment when nothing can be put right any more.
Reuben never got a chance to answer that sentence. His father said it, and died.

"Simeon and Levi are brothers. Their swords are weapons of violence. My soul, don't come into their council. My glory, don't be united to their assembly … Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel. I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel." (Genesis 49:5–7)
"Weapons of violence" is כְּלֵי חָמָס (*klei chamas*) — and that word חָמָס (*chamas*, violence) is exactly the sin of the generation before the flood in chapter 6.
And look how precise the wording of verse 7 is: "Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce" — what is cursed is their anger, not the two men.
Brothers and sisters, that is a mature rebuke: it goes after the deed, not the person.

When we are angry we do exactly the opposite — what we attack is usually the person himself: "You are just that sort of person." "You will never change as long as you live." That is not a rebuke. That is a verdict.
To let Jesus be King is to let his truth come through my mouth without my temper riding on it.
And there is one more thing worth saying. What did God eventually do with Levi's being scattered?

In Exodus chapter 32, over the matter of the golden calf, the sons of Levi took their stand on Moses' side. From that day the tribe of Levi was set apart for the priesthood, and they were settled here and there among the cities of Israel — teaching the law, carrying the holy office.
The same thing — being scattered. From a punishment, into a trust.
God can redeem the very worst thing about a man and turn it into his life's office. So when we talk about anybody's past, we leave a little room — and that includes when we talk about our own.
Why wait more than forty years — until his deathbed — to say it?

That line in chapter 35 is only a single line long: "While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard of it." At the time the text says only that he "heard of it" — he did not speak. More than forty years later he speaks, and Reuben never gets a chance to answer, because his father said it and died. This is the thing I want to put squarely in front of you: a matter that is never dealt with does not go away; it waits until the very last day, and then it gets said at the moment when nothing can be put right any more. So the words that need saying in a family should be said early, while both sides still have the strength to talk and the time to mend. Sitting on it is not gentleness. It is leaving the account for death to settle.
"Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce" — isn't that far too heavy a way to speak?

Look how precise the wording of verse 7 is: what is cursed is their anger, not the two men. That is a mature rebuke — it goes after the deed, not the person. When we are angry we do the very opposite: what we attack is usually the person himself, "you are just that sort of person", "you will never change as long as you live." That is not a rebuke; that is a verdict. To let Jesus be King is to let his truth come through my mouth without my temper riding on it. And in practice there is a simple check you can run: write down what you are about to say, circle every sentence shaped "you are …", and change them all to "that thing you did …". You will find that the force is still there and the wounding is gone.
2. A Light from the Original: The Scepter Will Not Depart from Judah
Then the camera turns to the fourth son.
"Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies. Your father's sons will bow down before you." (Genesis 49:8)
"Will praise you" is יוֹדוּךָ (*yoducha*) — and the name Judah itself, יְהוּדָה (*Yehudah*), means praise. When Leah bore him she said, "This time I will praise Yahweh."
"Will bow down before you" — that dream back in chapter 37 is spoken a second time, and this time it is spoken over Judah.
"Judah is a lion's cub. From the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down, he crouched as a lion, as a lioness. Who will rouse him up?" (Genesis 49:9)

"A lion's cub" is גּוּר אַרְיֵה (*gur aryeh*). Revelation chapter 5 says, "Behold, the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome." The root of that sentence is right here in this verse.
And then comes the summit of the chapter — and of the whole book of Genesis:
"The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs. The obedience of the peoples will be to him." (Genesis 49:10)

"Scepter" is שֵׁבֶט (*shevet*), which is both a ruling staff and the ordinary word for a tribe; "the ruler's staff" is מְחֹקֵק (*mechoqeq*), from a root meaning to engrave a decree — the staff of the one who lays down the law.

And the word שִׁילֹה (*Shiloh*) — the word standing behind the phrase the World English Bible renders "until he comes to whom it belongs" — is one of the most famous cruxes in the whole history of Old Testament interpretation. I am going to keep the rule of these notes: lay out the readings first, and give our judgement afterwards.

The first reading takes it as "the one to whom it belongs" — "until the one to whom it belongs comes." That comes of redividing the consonants (שֶׁלֹּה, *shelloh*), and the old Syriac version and many manuscripts support it.
The second reading works from the root meaning rest (שָׁלָה, *shalah*), and gives "the one who brings rest."
The third reading takes it as the place name Shiloh — the place where the tabernacle was once set up. But the grammar of this verse can hardly carry a place name.
The fourth reading gives "tribute to him", re-analysing the word as שַׁי לוֹ (*shai lo*).

The judgement of these notes is this: whichever reading you take, this verse points to one and the same thing — the kingship of Judah is to continue unbroken until one comes who is "the one to whom it belongs", "the one who brings rest", and the peoples are to give him their obedience.
And on this the ancient Jewish and the ancient Christian interpreters were headed in the same direction. The Talmud and the old Aramaic paraphrases both read this verse as a prophecy of the Messiah.
"The obedience of the peoples" is יִקְּהַת עַמִּים (*yiqqehat ammim*); this rare word occurs only twice in the whole Old Testament, and it means the obedience, the gathering-in, of the peoples.
Brothers and sisters, stop and think about who it is who is saying this.

An old man of a hundred and forty-seven, a few breaths from the end. No nation, no army, not one inch of ground of his own — the only property in his name is a cave for burying people in. His whole household is seventy souls, living as foreigners in somebody else's country on somebody else's relief.
And he says: the obedience of the peoples will be to him.
That is faith. Faith is not saying it once you can see it. Faith is saying it because God has said it.
And the picture in verse 11 is lovelier still:
"Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey's colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes."
Tying a donkey to a vine — what abundance that is, abundance enough that you can let a donkey chew its way through a grapevine. Washing your clothes in wine — what wealth that is.

And that donkey's colt, עִירֹה (*iroh*) — Zechariah chapter 9 says, "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! … Behold, your King comes to you! … lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey."
In Matthew chapter 21, on the day the Lord Jesus entered Jerusalem, what he rode was exactly that colt.
And the picture of clothes washed in "the blood of grapes" is taken up by Isaiah chapter 63, and taken up again by Revelation chapter 19 — the one who "is clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood."
A poem spoken by an old man on his sickbed runs all the way through to the day of the palm branches, and all the way to the cross.
"Until Shiloh comes" — how is that word Shiloh actually to be understood?

It is one of the most famous cruxes in the history of Old Testament interpretation, and there are four main readings. First, read it as "the one to whom it belongs", redividing the consonants; the old Syriac version and many manuscripts support this. Second, work from the root meaning rest and read "the one who brings rest." Third, take it as the place name Shiloh — although the grammar of this verse can hardly carry that. Fourth, read it as "tribute to him." The judgement of these notes is this: whichever reading you take, this verse points to one and the same thing — the kingship of Judah is to continue unbroken until one comes who is "the one to whom it belongs", "the one who brings rest", and the peoples are to give him their obedience.
An old man without one inch of land says "the obedience of the peoples will be to him." Is that faith, or is it empty words?

Think about the facts of his situation: a hundred and forty-seven years old and a few breaths from the end; no nation, no army, and the only property in his name a cave for burying people in; his whole household seventy souls, living as foreigners in somebody else's country on somebody else's relief. And he says: the obedience of the peoples will be to him. That is the very definition of faith — faith is not saying it once you can see it, it is saying it because God has said it. And that is intensely practical for us: the facts in your hands today cannot overrule what God has spoken. Of course we must keep one distinction clear. What is meant here is a promise God has actually spoken, not a wish of our own; putting the words "God said" on top of our own expectations is another matter altogether.
For the remaining tribes the text is brief, but every line of it is an act of seeing.

Zebulun "will dwell at the haven of the sea. He will be for a haven of ships" — and here is the interesting thing: the territory Zebulun was actually allotted later on did not touch the sea. And yet this tribe did in fact end up sitting on the trade routes.

Issachar is "a strong donkey, lying down between the saddlebags" — that is not an insult, it says the man can carry weight; only he "saw a resting place, that it was good", and would rather bow his shoulder to the burden and become a servant doing forced labour. Real strength, and yet the choice of an easy life: that is a very real danger.
"Dan will judge his people" — and the name Dan, דָּן, means precisely to judge. And the line that follows it, "Dan will be a serpent on the trail", is a picture with a warning in it.
And then at verse 18 a sentence that fits nowhere at all is suddenly dropped in:
"I have waited for your salvation, Yahweh." (Genesis 49:18)
Halfway through a long poem of blessing, the old man suddenly lifts his head and says a prayer to God.
It is the only time in the whole chapter that he speaks directly to God. And what he says is: I have waited for your salvation.
Brothers and sisters — a man who has been naming the future of twelve sons, one by one, stops in the middle of it to say: the thing I have been waiting for is your salvation.
He knows that those twelve tribes are not enough. The real answer does not lie with them.

"Joseph is a fruitful vine, a fruitful vine by a spring. His branches run over the wall … But his bow remained strong. The arms of his hands were made strong, by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, (from there is the shepherd, the stone of Israel)." (Genesis 49:22–24)
The shepherd, and the stone — this is the first time in the Bible that God is called a rock.
And the text records it honestly: "The archers have severely grieved him, shot at him, and persecuted him." The wounds Joseph took — his father knows about them now, and has said them out loud.
Wounded, and still bearing fruit; shot at, and the bow still strong. And the reason for it is not in himself; it is "the shepherd, the stone of Israel."
Last comes Benjamin: "Benjamin is a ravenous wolf." Out of this tribe came King Saul — and out of it came a Saul of Tarsus too.
Then verse 28 draws it all together: "All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them, and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his own blessing."
"According to his own blessing" — not one and the same sentence handed out to twelve men.
Here is the definition of a blessing: not saying something nice that would do for anybody, but saying what I truly see in this one particular person.
The other sons have far less said about them. Does that mean they matter less?

No. The length of each stanza in this poem reflects God's arrangement in the history of salvation, not a ranking of worth. And every stanza says something very concrete about that man's character and about the later situation of his tribe — which is exactly what makes it credible: a father who sees each of his children clearly, and says the good and the bad alike. There are two reminders in it for us. First, parents must truly know every one of their children, not only the one who is most like themselves. Second, do not measure your weight in God's heart by how many lines you were given. Your name is on the list, and that means you are remembered.
Finally the old man gives his instructions for what is to be done afterwards:

"I am to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite … There they buried Abraham and Sarah, his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah, his wife, and there I buried Leah." (Genesis 49:29–31)
He counts them off one at a time: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah — and then, Leah.
Brothers and sisters, that last name did not come easily.
The love of his life was Rachel. Rachel was buried by the roadside on the way to Ephrath, and after more than forty years he still remembers how far short of the end of that road she died.
And yet he chooses to be buried beside Leah.

Because that cave is not a grave; that cave is a promise. It is the one piece of property Abraham ever bought in the land of Canaan, and it is this family's one and only title deed in the land of promise.
He wants to go back to that cave — because it is the one small piece that actually belongs to him of the land he believes God will yet make good.
And in choosing this way he also does Leah a justice that came late. The elder sister whose "eyes were weak", the one who was not loved, lies in the end with him in the burying place of the fathers.
"When Jacob finished charging his sons, he gathered up his feet into the bed, breathed his last breath, and was gathered to his people." (Genesis 49:33)
"Was gathered to his people" is passive in the Hebrew — he does not go; he is taken.
A man who spent a whole lifetime grasping, at the last gathers up his feet into the bed.
Why was he so insistent on being buried in the cave of Machpelah?

Because that was the ground Abraham bought for four hundred shekels of silver — the only property this family legally owned in the land of promise. He spells out carefully who lies there: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and the place where he himself buried Leah. And notice that last clause — he lays himself down beside Leah, not beside Rachel. The man who loved Rachel all his life chooses at the end to lie beside the wife who was not loved. The text offers no explanation, and we do not need to supply one on his behalf; but that sentence reads like an old man's last act of amends and acknowledgement.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
There are several places in this chapter where we have to be particularly careful.

The first distortion is taking the prophecies over the tribes and matching them up with modern nations or modern personalities. This is a declaration about the later condition of the twelve tribes of Israel; it is not a code for telling people's fortunes, still less a tool for identifying which country or which regime today is which. Misused, it turns the pulpit into a prophecy show. The test is: when the congregation has heard you, do they stand in awe of God's word, or do they go away wanting to plug names into the slots?

The second distortion is preaching only Judah and skipping the three sons who come before him. Those three stanzas — Reuben, Simeon and Levi — are the settling of accounts on things this family left unaddressed for years. Skip them and the congregation never learns to deal with things today. The test is: when they have heard you, has anyone thought about that matter in his own family?

The third distortion is preaching "Shiloh" with flat certainty and never mentioning that it is disputed. This is one of the hardest words to translate in the whole Old Testament. Lay out the positions first, and then give your judgement — to hand over a conclusion without the working is to rob the people listening of their right to think.

The fourth distortion is preaching Levi's being scattered as nothing but a curse. From Exodus chapter 32 onwards the sons of Levi were set apart for the priesthood, and the scattering became a trust. Preach only the curse and the congregation will never see that God can redeem the worst thing about a person. The test is: when they have heard you, do they still believe God can turn somebody's past around?

The fifth distortion is treating the rebukes of this chapter as a manner of speaking that we may simply copy. Jacob said these things inside a prophetic declaration, and he said them and died — he never had to live with the aftermath. We do not stand where he stood. What we are to learn from him is his measure — the deed, not the person — not his tone of voice.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: our families are extremely good at saving things up for the very end. An elder keeps an account book in his heart, running for decades, and simply will not speak; and then it comes out on a sickbed, in a will, on the night before the funeral. And by then the person it is about has no chance to answer at all. That is exactly what happened to Reuben. Brothers and sisters, this week take one thing you have been putting off for a long time, spread it out before God first, and then set a date to go and talk about it. Talking while there is still a chance to answer is discipline; saying it once it is too late only leaves a wound behind.

The second question: we are very good at general, well-meaning words. At New Year we say "may you prosper"; at a wedding, "may you grow old together"; at a graduation, "may your future be bright." There is nothing wrong with any of them, and anybody at all could use them. Jacob blessed "everyone according to his own blessing" — he saw Reuben's recklessness, he saw Issachar's love of ease, he saw that Joseph had been shot at. This week, say to one person what you truly see in him, and let that be your blessing. Make it specific enough that the sentence could only ever be given to him.
7. Living 321 Out — the King Who Rode a Donkey's Colt into the City
Brothers and sisters, let us now tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. "The scepter will not depart from Judah … until he comes to whom it belongs." Revelation says, "the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome." And the next thing John sees is "a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain." A lion — and yet a lamb; holding the scepter and the ruler's staff — and yet riding a donkey's colt into the city. My role model is that King, and his way of winning runs in exactly the opposite direction from the world's.

The Bible is my standard. A standard is not "I will dare to say it once I have seen it"; a standard is "God has said it, so I believe it." An old man with no nation and no land says, the obedience of the peoples will be to him — that is not his optimism. That is God's word.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. To say out loud what is really there in a person, you need to see. To rebuke without wounding, you need measure. Neither of those is a technique. Rely on your intellect and lean on yourself and you will be tied in knots — you will spend the whole time polishing your wording. Rely on the heart and lean on the Spirit and you will have joy — he gives you the seeing, and he gives you the words that fit.

Let Jesus be King. What he cursed was their wrath, not the two men. Going after the deed and not the person is what a mature rebuke looks like. To let Jesus be King is to let his truth come through my mouth without my temper riding on it — because if the truth picks up my temper on the way out, all the hearer will remember is the temper.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The most moving sentence in the whole chapter is a prayer: "I have waited for your salvation, Yahweh." He knew that twelve sons were not enough, that the answer did not lie with them. To give God all the glory is to admit exactly this: nothing I hold in my hands can accomplish that thing. Only he can.

Establish God's system. "All these are the twelve tribes of Israel." Twelve men — a reckless one, a violent one, one who loved his ease, one who had been badly wounded. And God used them to establish his kingdom. To establish God's system is not to wait for perfect people; it is to use the people who are willing to let him be King.
Levi's being scattered was a punishment. How did it turn into the priestly tribe?

In Exodus chapter 32, over the matter of the golden calf, the sons of Levi took their stand on Moses' side. From that day the tribe of Levi was set apart for the priesthood, and they were settled here and there among the cities of Israel, teaching the law and carrying the holy office. The same thing — being scattered: from a punishment, into a trust. God can redeem the very worst thing about a man and turn it into his life's office. That is good news for two sorts of people. If you are still condemning yourself over your past, your story is not finished. And if you are busy passing judgement on somebody else, leave a little room. When we talk about anybody's past we have to remember that the very part we are talking about may be the place God intends to use.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, at the Same Bedside
We stand at that bedside carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "I was the one excelling in dignity." So was Reuben, once. He had the standing, he had the birth order, he had every qualification — and he could not hold himself still. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights: going up to his father's bed was precisely a grab at somebody else's place. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings and keeping inside the boundary God gave. Having the gift is not the hard part. Holding on to it is.

The fearful heart says, "I am afraid to hear what my elders really think of me." That verdict may be very hard to hear — and it may also be a piece of seeing that nobody has ever given you in your life. And brothers and sisters, the one who truly settles your worth is not any elder anywhere. It is the Lord who laid down his life for you.

The ashamed heart says, "That thing I did is written down, right there." What Simeon and Levi did was written down; what Reuben did was written down. And yet Levi later became the priestly tribe. God does not go back and edit the record. He rewrites the ending.

The wounded heart says, "The archers shot at me and persecuted me." That sentence is in the Bible, and it is a father saying it on Joseph's behalf. God has seen your wound, and he has said it out loud. And then the same passage goes straight on: "But his bow remained strong." You are still standing, and not because you are the stronger sort — because of that shepherd, that stone.
Four kinds of heart, at the same bedside. And the father who has said and heard all of it stops halfway through to say one thing: I have waited for your salvation, Yahweh.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, towards God. Take one thing you have been putting off for a long time and spread it out before God. Do not ask him to deal with it for you; ask first for the courage to face it, and for the right moment.

Second, towards yourself. Check whether you have been turning rebuke into a rejection of the person. Think back to the last time you were angry and what you said — were you attacking the thing that was done, or the one who did it?
Third, towards others. Say to one person what you truly see in him, and let that be your blessing. Be specific — specific enough that the sentence belongs to him and to nobody else.
Fourth, towards daily living. This week, do not fob anybody off with a general, well-meaning phrase. Either say it in earnest, or do not say it yet.

Fifth, towards the mission. Speak God's promise to the next generation, even while there is still nothing to see. When Jacob said the obedience of the peoples will be to him, his household numbered seventy.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is an old man in the Bible who is about to die, whose whole household is seventy people, living as foreigners in somebody else's country. Second: he said that out of his descendants a King would come, and that all the peoples would give him their obedience. Third: seventeen hundred years later that King rode a donkey's colt into Jerusalem — and those words were written down before he was ever born.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer save the words that need saying for the day when it is too late.
I declare that what I rebuke is the deed and not the person; that truth comes through my mouth without my temper riding on it.
I declare that I will bless people according to each one's own blessing, saying what I truly see.
I declare that what I have waited for is the salvation of Yahweh; the scepter will not depart from Judah, and that One will surely come.
Those pictures in verse 11 — what have they to do with the Lord Jesus?

There are three direct lines. First, the donkey's colt — Zechariah chapter 9 says, "Behold, your King comes to you! … lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey", and in Matthew chapter 21 what the Lord Jesus rode into Jerusalem was exactly that colt. Second, the picture of clothes washed in "the blood of grapes" is taken up by Isaiah chapter 63 and taken up again by Revelation chapter 19 — the one who "is clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood." Third, verse 9's "Judah is a lion's cub" — Revelation chapter 5 says, "the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome." A dying man's blessing, with the threads of the whole Bible buried inside it.

One man's life: it begins with a hand grasping his brother's heel; in the middle come twenty years of running, one night of wrestling, twenty-two years of grief over a lost son, and seventeen years of old age lived as a foreigner in another man's land. And at the end he gathers up his feet into the bed, and breathes his last.

And in the last words he left behind there is one sentence that runs like this: the scepter will not depart from Judah, until he comes to whom it belongs, and the obedience of the peoples will be to him.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because of the twelve sons in this chapter there is not one who can carry that promise: the reckless one, the violent one, the one who loved his ease, the wounded one — none of them is enough. Which is why that old man stopped in the middle of it, lifted his head and said: I have waited for your salvation, Yahweh. And that salvation did in the end come — riding a donkey's colt, passing through the palm branches, walking up a hill; and he turned out to be the Lion who has overcome, and also the Lamb who was slain.

May God bless every one of us: while there is still time, to say clearly the words that need saying; when we bless people, to say what we truly see; and though we can see nothing yet, still to dare to speak God's promise to the next generation. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ A matter that is never dealt with waits until the moment when nothing can be put right, and only then gets said. Is there something like that in your family?
2. ★★ What was cursed was "their anger", not the two men. What is the difference between a rebuke and a verdict?
3. ★ Levi's being scattered went from a punishment to a trust. What does that do to the way you look at your own past?
4. ★★ An old man without one inch of land said, the obedience of the peoples will be to him. Is faith saying it once you can see it, or saying it because God has said it?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (my branch of the family is the blessed one), fearful (I am afraid to hear what my elders really think of me), ashamed (I am like Reuben; one thing settled my whole life), wounded (nobody has ever blessed me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "The scepter will not depart from Judah … until he comes to whom it belongs." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a sentence inside you that ought to have been said and never has been? What is it that has been stopping you?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The one thing I would least want to leave until the very end to say is …"
9. ★★ This week, to whom are you going to say that sentence? Give the name, the time, and how the first line will begin.

Leader's reminder: this lesson will touch on elders' verdicts and on family judgements that have stood for years. Do not let group members pass comment on one another's families. If someone has been held for a long time under one old sentence, stay with him first, and follow up with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, which do you say more often — "you are just that sort of person", or "that thing you did"? Name the sentence you are going to change.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, who has been tied up for years by one old remark?

12. ★★★ Practising the deed and not the person: this week, write down the rebuke you mean to give, and change every "you are …" into "that thing you did …". Say now what the matter is that you have to raise.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him this week to pull you up whenever you mix the person and the deed together in one telling-off. Say his name here and now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is an old man in the Bible who called his twelve sons to his bedside as he was dying and told each one the truth about himself, the good and the bad alike. Second, he owned nothing at all, and yet he said to his fourth son, the obedience of the peoples will be to him — and that word was fulfilled later on in Jesus. Third, so what I have learned is this: say what needs saying early, and do not leave it to the last day. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the sentence you have never said, and the way of speaking you are going to change. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to make us say what needs saying while there is still time, and to keep our own anger out of it when we have to rebuke someone.
